paras: The lynching of Frank Craft, William Underwood and James Butler took place on the night of July 1, 1881, when a mob took the three men from the Dade County jail at Greenfield, Missouri, and hanged them in the yard. The three were held as members of a gang of horse thieves whose leader, Taylor Underwood, was accused of killing a deputy sheriff named McElrath. The story ran as a brief wire item in July and returned to print in August, when Taylor Underwood was arrested and an armed crowd gathered at Greenfield on his return.

Dispatches described the three prisoners as members of a gang of horse thieves and "desperadoes" in southwest Missouri. According to a St. Louis dispatch of July 3, the gang's leader, Taylor Underwood, had killed Deputy Sheriff McElrath at "Greenville" a few days earlier while McElrath was trying to arrest him, and was still at large with officers in pursuit.

According to the Springfield dispatch, at about 11 p.m. an "infuriated mob" went to the house of Sheriff Whiteside, bound him, and took the keys of the jail. The mob then took Craft, William Underwood and Butler out of the jail into the court-yard and hanged them to trees until they were dead. A fourth prisoner, Mitchell, was left in his cell because, the dispatch said, the mob thought he would be needed as a witness against gang members still at large.
The St. Louis wire put the mob at about fifty "disguised men" and said the three were hanged to a tree in the jail-yard; another brief called them "masked men."

Taylor Underwood was arrested at Carthage, Missouri, about August 5, after what a Carthage dispatch called "a desperate struggle" with Detective E. S. Pike. The same dispatch, credited to the St. Louis Republican's Carthage correspondent, said three of Underwood's gang "were lynched by citizens of Dade County for being concerned in the murder of McElrath."

On August 11, Sheriff Roberts of Jasper County, Pike and two assistants brought Underwood by rail to Greenfield, according to a Springfield dispatch to the Memphis Daily Appeal. About 150 armed men gathered on the hill above the depot, "all seemingly thirsty for Underwood's blood," but a posse of twenty-five men raised by Sheriff Whiteside escorted the prisoner by coach into town, and the dispatch reported that "law and order prevailed."
No report of an inquest, of arrests of the lynchers, or of any prosecution appears in the coverage.

White papers carried the July lynching as a short item in news summaries, from Pennsylvania and Ohio to Georgia, Alabama, Arkansas and Mississippi. Headlines were plain, such as the Stark County Democrat's "Three Desperadoes Lynched" and "Lynching" in two Ohio weeklies. The Chicago Tribune ran its dispatch under "Lynch Law" and described the hanging as the summoning of the "miscreants" to "the bar of Judge Lynch." None of the reports gave the race of the three men, who were identified only as horse thieves and desperadoes.

In August the arrest wire ran under headlines such as "Capture of a Desperado," "Important Capture" and "Arrest of Underwood, the Murderer," and the New North-west in Montana headed it "Lynching Desperadoes." These items called Underwood McElrath's "murderer" without qualification. The Memphis Daily Appeal's account of the August crowd credited the "vigilance" of Sheriff Whiteside and his posse for keeping the peace.

The St. Louis wire put the jail at "Springfield, Dade county," but the more detailed dispatch, which named the sheriff and the spared prisoner, and later reports placed it at Greenfield. July reports dated the lynching to Friday night or the night of the 1st, while the Memphis Daily Appeal in August gave the second. Accounts of McElrath's death also differed, with July reports placing it "a few days" before the lynching and the August wire "three months ago," and the Tribune calling him a marshal rather than a deputy sheriff.

Taylor Underwood's own fate was misreported: the Eaton Democrat said he was "lynched at Carthage" and the Fremont County Record that he was "killed by a detective." The Memphis Daily Appeal's later and more detailed account of his delivery to Greenfield shows him alive in custody.

accounts.label: Springfield dispatch (Chicago Tribune)
accounts.gist: At Greenfield about 11 p.m. an 'infuriated mob' bound Sheriff Whiteside, took the keys, and hanged Craft, W. Underwood and Butler to trees in the court-yard, sparing Mitchell as a witness.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: About fifty disguised men took the three from the jail at 'Springfield, Dade county' on Friday night and hanged them to a tree in the jail-yard; Taylor Underwood, accused of killing McElrath, was at large.

accounts.label: Carthage special (August wire)
accounts.gist: Taylor Underwood was arrested at Carthage after a struggle with Detective Pike; three of his gang had been lynched by Dade County citizens for being concerned in McElrath's murder.

accounts.label: Springfield dispatch (Memphis Appeal)
accounts.gist: Underwood was brought back to Greenfield by rail; about 150 armed men gathered, but Sheriff Whiteside's posse of 25 protected him.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune ran it under 'Lynch Law', calling the victims 'miscreants' summoned 'to the bar of Judge Lynch' after public feeling 'culminated', while calling the mob 'infuriated'.
Most papers ran the July item as a one-paragraph summary or under plain heads such as 'Three Desperadoes Lynched' and 'Lynching'.
August heads ('Capture of a Desperado', 'A Desperado in the Toils') called Underwood the murderer of McElrath and tied the lynching to that killing.
The Memphis Appeal credited 'the vigilance' of Sheriff Whiteside and his posse for keeping order when an armed crowd gathered for Underwood.

conflicts.note: The more detailed dispatch, naming the sheriff and the spared prisoner, and the later Memphis account both place it at Greenfield; the 'Springfield' wire may have taken the dispatch's dateline.
The contemporary July reports agree on the night of the 1st; the August recap says the 2d.
